disposition.reason: Developer appealed the Norwich DRB's denial of an after-the-fact zoning permit for a single-family dwelling on parcel 2; the dispute decides whether a residential use may lawfully exist on that lot at all, so it concerns permission for new housing.

evidence.quote: Docket No. 77‐4‐05 Vtec concerns an appeal filed by Developer from a decision of the Town of Norwich Development Review Board (DRB), denying his application for
an after‐the‐fact zoning permit to construct a single‐family dwelling at 84 Elm Street.
the zoning regulations prohibit more than one residential use per lot and a permit may not be issued.

project.description: After-the-fact zoning permit for a two-story L-shaped single-family house already built (1999-2000) on parcel 2 at 84 Elm Street, Village Residential district.

evidence.quote: In his 2005 application, Developer seeks permit approval for the previously constructed “L‐shaped” single‐family residence on parcel 2.
Developer constructed a single‐family dwelling on parcel 2 in 1999‐2000 without first obtaining a final determination
the residential development of a parcel of land in the Town of Norwich (Town).

municipal_decision.description: The DRB granted Neighbor's appeal of the Zoning Administrator's January 18, 2005 approval and overturned the permit, denying the application.

evidence.quote: Neighbor appealed that approval to the DRB, which granted his appeal and overturned the permit approval by its Decision on April 1, 2005.
Appellant Paul Nowicki (hereinafter Developer) is represented by Gerald R. Tarrant, Esq.;
Developer filed his notice of appeal of the DRB’s denial with this Court on April 15, 2005.

discretion.description: The appeal turned on statutory interpretation of the existing-small-lot provision (24 V.S.A. 4412(2)), merger of parcels, which law applies, and the fixed rule allowing one residential use per lot.

evidence.quote: The parties’ disputes center for the most part on the interpretation of the applicable legal standards.
As the issue is a legal one, we review it de novo on appeal.
the separate development of parcel 2 is prohibited by § 10.1.3 of the Zoning Regulations, which forbids more than one residential use per lot.

observed_status.description: Permit denied; the Environmental Court granted Neighbor summary judgment and the Supreme Court affirmed. A separate enforcement action (another docket) remained pending.

evidence.quote: Neighbor’s cross‐motion for summary judgment in Docket No. 77‐4‐05 Vtec is GRANTED, as Developer’s zoning permit application cannot be granted under any factual scenario

judgments.note: Clearly a municipal appeal. Housing rests on the after-the-fact row: the house exists, but the ruling that only one residential use is allowed per lot means its lawful residential use is what is at stake, not a mere paperwork permit. Occupancy is not stated in so many words.
After-the-fact permit for an existing house; treated as occupancy at stake because denial bars the residential use of parcel 2 and an enforcement action over the house followed.
Start exact (April 15, 2005 notice of appeal). The Supreme Court's affirmance is the conclusion but undated beyond 'May Term, 2007', so end is on_or_after 2007-05-01; at_least 746 days.

One single-family dwelling; existing physical house is not authorization, so counted as the proposed unit.
All Statement of Questions issues are statutory interpretation and fixed rules (lot merger, one residential use per lot); the takings claim is legal too.
Shared Environmental Court decision also decides 156-8-05 and 220-10-05; nothing from those dockets is carried into this record beyond naming them.
